title: Write grant record — v1.0
description: One line of ci/results/protected-writes.jsonl, written only by `ligature authorize-write` (chainlink #114). A grant is a CAPABILITY RECORD: an issue-scoped authorization for one bounded write into a declared protected root, so a protected write that is genuinely sanctioned does not need `allowed_roots` widened (#103's enforcement left that write with only two routes, both worse -- widen the root, or hand-edit a file outside every tool). It is not a permission surface: the fields below are the whole of what a grant authorizes, every one of them is recomputed by the consumer (`scripts/write_authorization.parse_grant`) rather than trusted, and a recomputed disagreement authorizes nothing. Closed (`additionalProperties: false`) with the same discipline chainlink #104 applied to `verifier_policy`: a key nobody reads must not validate as if it authorized something. This schema states the shape; the CONSUMER states the semantics -- notably `expires_at == issued_at + ttl_seconds` and `grant_id == sha256(the binding fields)[:12]`, neither of which JSON Schema can express, and both of which `parse_grant` recomputes on every read. Trust model: an audit trail, not a signature. A line appended by someone with write access to `ci/results/` is indistinguishable from one `authorize-write` wrote -- that access is itself outside the agent's write set, and `authorize-write` refuses to record anything at all when this ledger is inside a declared protected root. The CONSUMER holds that same refusal rather than trusting the writer to have been the one that wrote the line: `write-set-check` reports every record read from such a ledger with status `ledger-protected` and honors none of them, because a capability trail inside a protected root must not be able to authorize writes there -- including, by a grant naming this ledger's own path, to vouch for its own presence in the very protected surface it has to stay outside of.

event.description: The ledger is a trail of events; a line whose `event` is anything else is not an authorization record and is never read as one.

schema_version.description: Versioned like every other artifact schema in this pipeline (docs/trust-and-compatibility-boundaries.md §1/§3): a breaking change to the record's shape takes a new value and a migration note.

grant_id.description: `GW-` plus the first 12 hex digits of the sha256 over the canonical JSON of the fields the grant's authority is OF -- issue, path, path_kind, op, one_shot, issuer, issuer_kind, issued_at, ttl_seconds (never `note`, which authorizes nothing and must not be able to invalidate a real record either, and there is no separate append timestamp to include: `issued_at` says when the grant was issued, and a second clock reading would be one more value a hand-written line could disagree with for no gain). Recomputed on read: a record edited in place to authorize a different path, issue, operation, issuer or expiry under a preserved id is rejected, which is what makes the ledger an audit trail rather than an editable permission file. Also the anti-replay key -- `authorize-write` refuses to record an id the ledger already holds, so re-running the issuing command with the same `--issued-at` is idempotent.

issue.description: The issue this grant is scoped to. A grant authorizes ITS OWN issue only, which is why `write-set-check`, `status` and `check` all take `--issue N`; with no `--issue`, no grant is consulted at all and the write-set verdict is the pre-#114 one (fail-closed rather than permissive).

path.description: The workspace-relative path this grant covers. Syntactically checked, never resolved against the filesystem: the write does not exist yet when the grant is issued, and resolving would make a grant depend on a symlink someone could retarget. An absolute path, a `..` segment, and a trailing `/` (a directory) are all refused -- the same escape rule `validate_work_package.check_write_set_anchoring` applies to a declared write-set pattern. `path_kind: pattern` makes it a glob instead, and then it must be explicitly bounded: a literal (non-wildcard) segment is required and the vacuous shapes (`**`, `*/*`) are refused, because a grant is a capability and a pattern with no anchor is a standing permission over the workspace.

path_kind.description: `exact` covers one file; `pattern` covers the files the (bounded) glob names. Recomputed from `path` on read and required to agree, so a record cannot declare a pattern to be an exact file -- or an exact file to be a pattern.

op.description: Closed vocabulary: a grant authorizes exactly the one operation it names, which is what 'a grant cannot authorize another operation' means. `write` covers creating or replacing the content -- the only operation `write-set-check` consumes, because a file's presence is what a file walk can observe (create and replace are indistinguishable here, and the record says so rather than pretending otherwise). `delete` authorizes removing the granted path and is recorded so a sanctioned deletion is auditable; it can never make an existing file clean, since an absent file is not an observable this check reports on.

one_shot.description: `true` binds one exact file rather than a standing grant for the TTL, and is refused on `path_kind: pattern` (a pattern authorizes as many writes as its TTL allows). `write-set-check` reports the write it authorized with status `spent` in `authorized_writes[]` instead of `active` (the grant itself stays `active` in the report's ledger audit until it expires, because until then it still covers the one path it names): an attribution, NOT a consumed count. A workspace snapshot observes which files exist, not how many times each was written, so the check cannot tell the write a one-shot grant authorized from a later edit to the same file -- it says so in `details` rather than letting `spent` imply a counter it never kept, and the grant's own `expires_at` is the bound on how long the attribution stands. A file needing further sanctioned writes needs a further grant: each is its own append-only record.

issuer.description: The named identity that issued the grant. Required with no default and no LLM-supplied value, exactly like `approve`'s `--reviewer`: a grant with no named issuer is not a capability record, and prose about who approved it is not an issuer.

issuer_kind.description: Which lane issued it. `human` (the default) is a human checkpoint on the same terms as `approve`/`accept-policy`/`record-ruling` -- the installed skill says an agent must never run it. `supervisor` is the automation lane, reachable only for an identity the descriptor declares in `write_set.authorized_supervisors`, and re-verified against that whitelist EVERY time a consumer honors the record: withdrawing the identity from the descriptor withdraws the grant on the next run, and a hand-written record naming an undeclared supervisor authorizes nothing. No unbounded LLM prose permission exists in either lane.

issued_at.description: ISO-8601 with an explicit UTC offset; a naive timestamp is refused, because 'expired' is not decidable against a clock with no offset. `--issued-at` sets it explicitly so a re-run of the issuing command produces the same `grant_id` (idempotent) and so an expiring grant is reproducible without waiting; a timestamp in the future is refused, because a grant cannot be issued for a time that has not happened. The CONSUMER decides the other end of the window against its own clock: a record whose `issued_at` is still ahead of it is reported `not-yet-issued` and authorizes nothing, so a hand-appended future-dated line is not 'unexpired' merely because it satisfies `expires_at == issued_at + ttl_seconds`.

ttl_seconds.description: How long the grant authorizes a write, in seconds. Bounded on both ends: `authorize-write` refuses a non-positive value and anything above 86400, and `parse_grant` recomputes both bounds on every read -- so a hand-appended line naming a year's authority with a self-consistent `expires_at` is rejected rather than honored. The default is 900 -- a grant is issued for the work at hand, never standing by default.

expires_at.description: `issued_at + ttl_seconds`, recomputed on read together with `ttl_seconds`'s own bounds: a record claiming more time than it was granted is rejected ('a grant cannot outlive its TTL'), as is one naming a TTL no issuer could have been granted, and an expired one authorizes nothing while being reported as `expired` rather than dropped. `write-set-check` treats `now >= expires_at` as expired (the boundary is inclusive, decided against the run's own clock -- no sleeping and no clock race, which is what lets a re-run of the same command report the same verdict for the same bytes).

note.description: Free-text audit metadata, or null. Recorded and never read back as authority: no prose field is consulted when deciding whether a grant authorizes a write, and it is excluded from `grant_id` so it can neither create an authorization nor invalidate a real one.
